newsitem.title: FRANCE: When Moshe Dayan walked the streets of Hebron.
newsitem.headline: When Moshe Dayan walked the streets of Hebron.

text.p: When Moshe Dayan, Israel's one-eyed hero, toured Hebron's crowded casbah nearly 30 years ago, local residents saw him as an occupying enemy but were thrilled to come face-to-face with a legend.
Palestinian merchants excitedly called to each other as Dayan sauntered through the dusty market's crowded stalls and jostled with one another to shake his hand as he extended greetings in Arabic.
The atmosphere was far less jocular on Friday when Israeli troops pulled out of most of the town with local youths hurling insults after them.

Dayan, then Israel's Defence Minister and flush from his victory in the June 1967 "Six-Day War," made several visits to Hebron in the early years of the occupation when he apparently regarded himself as a sort of Israeli "Lawrence of Arabia" seeking to build ties with local leaders.

As a Reuters correspondent, I accompanied Dayan on one such visit in the late 1960s when he came to welcome back from Jordan the town's mayor and most influential clan leader, the ageing but impressive-looking Sheikh Muhammed Ali Jaabari.
Both Israel and Jordan paid court to Jaabari, seen as a possible bulwark against the growing influence of what both states saw as leftist groups, which then included Yasser Arafat's Fatah movement.

Israeli "civil affairs" officers told reporters they were sure Jaabari, whose strict brand of Islam kept the town free of such modern amenities as cinemas, would enter an alliance with the Jewish state.
But the wily and cautious Jaabari spoke little and mostly nodded his head when pressed by reporters.
Hebron was then perhaps the most carefully preserved and least developed town on the West Bank, and surely the one closest to what the area may have looked like in Biblical times.

Virtually all local residents wore long flowing gowns instead of Western-style clothes as today, some still wore "tarboosh" hats and camels were not an uncommon scene in the pungent-smelling fly-infested market.
The handful of Jewish settlers fit easily into the courtyard of the Taggart fort overlooking the town where they were squatters after the army hauled them out of a hotel in the town centre.
One of their leaders was already the feverish-looking Rabbi Moshe Levinger, today still the nemesis of Hebron's Arab population.
The Hebron settlers were to draw some odd characters including a descendant of Jaabari who converted to Judaism and a great nephew of the Soviet revolutionary leader Leon Trotsky, born Lev Bronstein.
The Palestinian population was stunned by the 1967 defeat and Israeli tourists then walked safely in the town, a sight which disappeared many years ago.

Pressed by reporters for his view of the situation, the aged Jaarbari, who died in 1976, stroked his beard and allowed that he had "seen the Turks here, and the British and the Jordanians and now the Israelis."
The implication was that like the others before them, the Israelis would one day also leave.
